nameStory: The 'three-awn' name comes from the distinctive three bristle-like projections (called awns) that stick out from each seed, making them look like tiny pitchforks. 'Oldfield' refers to its habit of quickly colonizing abandoned agricultural fields and disturbed areas. It's also called 'ant rice' because ants love to collect and store the small, rice-like seeds.
description: Oldfield Three-awn is a slender annual grass that forms loose clumps of branching stems reaching 1 to 2 feet tall. The whole plant has an airy, delicate appearance with gray-green stems often tinged with purple. Its most distinctive feature is the seed heads, which contain numerous small seeds each topped with three long, spreading bristles that give the plant a spiky, almost fuzzy look from a distance.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Each tiny seed is crowned with three spreading bristles (awns) - one center bristle up to 3 inches long and two shorter side bristles, creating a distinctive three-pronged fork appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose, airy clumps of thin, branching stems that feel delicate and bend easily in your fingers, giving the whole plant a wispy appearance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, gray-green stems with purple tinges that branch repeatedly, feeling smooth and somewhat wiry to the touch

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Open, spreading clusters of spikelets that create an airy, cloud-like appearance, especially when backlit by sun

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that are typically rolled inward and feel rough along the edges when you run your finger along them

habitat: Look for Oldfield Three-awn in dry, sandy or gravelly soils in disturbed areas like old fields, roadsides, railroad tracks, and areas recovering from burns. It thrives in sunny, open locations where other plants struggle to establish, particularly in poor soils that drain quickly.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small grass clumps with narrow leaves, easily overlooked among other grasses starting their growth.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin developing their characteristic branching seed heads, with purple tints becoming more noticeable on stems.
seasonality.fall: This is prime identification time as the three-awned seeds are fully developed and most visible, creating the plant's distinctive spiky appearance.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with some seeds still attached, appearing as brittle, tan-colored clumps that rattle in the wind.

funFact: The three bristles on each seed aren't just for show - they work like tiny grappling hooks, allowing the seeds to literally climb into ant colonies where they're stored as food, giving the plant free seed dispersal and underground protection!
confusionNotes: Other three-awn grasses in the same genus look very similar, but Oldfield Three-awn is typically the most branched and delicate-looking of the group. The key is counting those three bristles per seed - if you see just one or two bristles, you're looking at a different grass entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'prairie' grass by some, this species is actually more of an opportunist that quickly colonizes any disturbed ground, making it quite different from true prairie grasses that form stable, long-term communities.
compareHints: Among its three-awn relatives in New England, Oldfield Three-awn is the most delicate and branched, with the most open, airy seed heads. Seaside Threeawn grows in coastal areas and is more robust, while Arrowfeather Threeawn tends to be taller and less branched. The branching pattern and overall delicate appearance help distinguish this species from its sturdier cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the three-awn grasses in New England, Slim-spike has the most delicate, narrow flower spikes - much thinner than the more robust spikes of Arrowfeather Threeawn or the branched clusters of Fork-tip Three-awn.

Arrowfeather threeawn is typically taller and more robust than most of its relatives like fork-tip three-awn, and its seed bristles are usually longer and more feathery than the shorter, stiffer bristles of oldfield three-awn.
Among New England's three-awn grasses, fork-tip three-awn is unique for its distinctly forked branching pattern and smaller size.
Seaside Threeawn is distinguished from other New England threeawns primarily by its coastal habitat - it's the only species in the genus that grows directly in beach sand and tolerates salt spray.
Among New England's three-awn grasses, forked three-awn is distinguished by its branching pattern from the base rather than higher up the stem like fork-tip three-awn.
